name: Cuneus Equitum Clibanariorum Palmirenorum

abilities.name: Wedge
abilities.text: The unit moves into a wedge-shaped attack formation.

abilities.name: Trample
abilities.text: Charges are more effective for an extended time.

attributes.name: Disciplined
attributes.text: This unit does not suffer a morale penalty when the general dies. It can also rally after routing more often.

attributes.name: Fire Whilst Moving
attributes.text: This unit can fire when mounted and moving.

attributes.name: Parthian Shot
attributes.text: This unit can fire all around and not just in-front of itself.

attributes.name: Scare (everyone)
attributes.text: This unit frightens all enemy units.

attributes.name: Immune to Fear
attributes.text: This unit is immune to the fear effects of scary units.

short: The name Palmirenorum - refers to a unit recruited from local inhabitants of the town of Palmyra. Cuneus equitum - a spearhead, a wedge of horsemen, it is a wedge-shaped battle formation used to concentrate the onslaught and break through the enemy formation. It is assumed that the cunei were separated by Constantine I from the equites which were formed under Diocletian on the basis of the old cavalry units. The fact that several units of cuneus have received the status of Comitatenses (according to Notita Dignitatum), can testify about high combat efficiency of these units. Most likely these units were armed with contus (Ancient Greek kontos, «bear spear»; Latin contus) - a huge spear. The Clibanarii are considered to be of Parthian-Sasanian origin. The etymology of the term comes from the Greek klibanos or Latin clibanu, meaning «oven», «roaster for baking bread», which seems an appropriate analogy for a warrior in heavy armor fighting in the hot Eastern climate. If we refer to the Notitia Dignitatum, we see that the status of the clibanarii was higher than the one of the cataphractarii. According to F. Altheim, the clibanarii were covered with armor from head to toe and their horses also were fully protected by armor.
history: The skill required to fire a bow from a moving horse is phenomenal. Ancient cavalry archers had to keep control of their mounts with their knees whilst using both arms to fire their bows, which took a great deal of practice and physical strength. Often lightly armoured, horse archers were the ideal skirmish troops as they could quickly reach key areas of the battlefield to harass the enemy, but without getting so close they were forced into melee. Nomadic tribes, such as the Sarmatians and Huns, were renowned for their skilled riders and used horse archers to great effect. The combination of skill and the deadly composite bow, which could puncture straight through armour, made their horsemen the dread of all those they encountered.
strengths: Very low damage and armour penetration
